title: Overlap and multiplication identities on Weyl translates of the open cell
statement:
Let $A$ be a nonzero commutative ring and $P=(G,T=D_A(M),\Phi,\Phi^\vee,\Delta,(X_\alpha))$ a pinned split realization [def-sfb-pinned-split-root-realization]. Use the root subgroups $U_c$, representatives $n_\alpha$, Weyl group $W=N_G(T)/T$, groups $U^\pm=U_{\pm\Phi^+}$, and open cell $\Omega=U^-TU^+$ of [lem-sfb-split-root-subgroup-weyl-calculus]. Here $N=N_G(T)$ is the subgroup scheme whose points normalize $T$ after every further algebra extension. For a simple root put $L_\alpha=M\cap\mathbf Q\alpha$, $S_\alpha=D_A(M/L_\alpha)\subset T$ and $K_\alpha=Z_G(S_\alpha)$; this centralizer consists of the points commuting with $S_\alpha$ after every further algebra extension. Let $H$ be an affine $A$-group scheme, meaning an affine scheme over $\operatorname{Spec}A$ with multiplication, identity and inverse satisfying the group diagrams. All homomorphisms preserve these operations.
Give homomorphisms $f_N:N\to H$ and $F_\pm:U^\pm\to H$, and put $f_T=f_N|_T$ and $g_c=F_+|_{U_c}$ for positive $c$, $g_c=F_-|_{U_c}$ for negative $c$. Suppose that, on every commutative $A$-algebra $R$, for $n\in N(R)$ with Weyl image $w$ and $u\in U_c(R)$, one has
$$f_N(n)g_c(u)f_N(n)^{-1}=g_{wc}(nun^{-1}),$$
interpreted on open-and-closed parts when $w$ is locally constant. Suppose for every simple $\alpha$ there is a homomorphism $E_\alpha:K_\alpha\to H$ restricting to $g_{\pm\alpha}$ on $U_{\pm\alpha}$ and to $f_N$ on $N\cap K_\alpha$.
For each $w\in W$ choose a representative $n_w\in N(A)$ which is a word in the $n_\alpha$, choosing $n_1=1$. Set $C_w=n_w\Omega$ and define the $A$-morphism $a_w:C_w\to H$ by
$$a_w(n_wvtu)=f_N(n_w)F_-(v)f_T(t)F_+(u),\qquad v\in U^-,\ t\in T,\ u\in U^+.$$
Then the $C_w$ form an open cover of $G$, and $a_w=a_z$ on the scheme-theoretic open intersections $C_w\cap C_z$. If $\mu:G\times_A G\to G$ is multiplication and $p_1,p_2$ are the projections, then for every $w,z,r\in W$ the morphism identity
$$a_r\circ\mu=(a_w\circ p_1)(a_z\circ p_2)$$
holds on $(C_w\times_A C_z)\cap\mu^{-1}(C_r)$, where the product on the right is multiplication in $H$. These conclusions permit empty roots and nonreduced and disconnected $A$. No rank-two subgroup homomorphisms are part of the data.

Technical local formulation of the omitted induction; formulated by the agent. Read online; archival literature copy WANTED. No Stacks tag states this reductive/root-system result.

proof.text:
Write $a:\Omega\to H$ for $a_1$. Normalizer equivariance for $t\in T$ extends from each root subgroup to $U^\pm$ by their ordered-product coordinates. Thus $B^-=U^-T$ and $B^+=TU^+$ have their semidirect-product group laws, and the formulas $F_-(v)f_T(t)$ and $f_T(t)F_+(u)$ define homomorphisms on them. In particular
$$a(b_-x b_+)=f_{B^-}(b_-)a(x)f_{B^+}(b_+)$$
for $x\in\Omega$, since multiplying on the left by $U^-T$ or on the right by $TU^+$ preserves the displayed cell coordinates. This is an identity on all algebra points: move a torus factor past an ordered root product and use the given homomorphism laws. All the formulas below are morphisms, not just formulas on field points.

source.place: Theorem 6.2.1 proof, printed p.199: the map on the open cell after the unipotent homomorphisms have been constructed.

proof.text: Over an algebraically closed $A$-field $F$, apply the inversion-root Bruhat factorization. A geometric point has the form $v n_w t u$ with $v\in U_{I_w}$. Conjugation by $n_w^{-1}$ carries every root factor of $v$ into $U^-$, because $w^{-1}I_w\subset-\Phi^+$. Hence the point belongs to $n_w\Omega$. This proves that the open subschemes $C_w$ cover every geometric fibre and thus all of $G$: every point of $G$ lifts to a geometric point of its fibre. The representative used in the factorization may be the chosen word $n_w$, as its statement permits arbitrary representatives.

source.place: Theorem 1.4.12 and Corollary 1.4.14, printed pp.38--39, applied to geometric fibres as in Theorem 6.2.1, p.199.

proof.text:
For a simple $\alpha$ use the rank-one enlargement $J_\alpha$ and its unique coordinates $vku$. Define
$$b_\alpha(vku)=F_-(v)E_\alpha(k)F_+(u).$$
Its restriction to $\Omega$ is $a$: in the smaller chart write $k=x_-t x_+$ and use the restrictions of $E_\alpha$ and the homomorphism properties of $F_\pm$. The reflection $s_\alpha$ permutes $\Phi^+\setminus\{\alpha\}$: it changes only the coefficient of $\alpha$, while any other positive root has a positive coefficient at another simple root; sign coherence makes its reflected root positive and different from $\alpha$. The same holds negatively. Root calculus therefore shows that $n_\alpha$ normalizes $V_\alpha^\pm$; also $n_\alpha\in K_\alpha$. Thus left multiplication by $n_\alpha$ preserves $J_\alpha$, and on it
$$b_\alpha(n_\alpha vku)=F_-(n_\alpha v n_\alpha^{-1})E_\alpha(n_\alpha k)F_+(u)=f_N(n_\alpha)b_\alpha(vku).$$
The last equality follows from normalizer equivariance on the ordered negative root factors and from $E_\alpha(n_\alpha)=f_N(n_\alpha)$. Restricting gives $a(n_\alpha x)=f_N(n_\alpha)a(x)$ wherever both $x$ and $n_\alpha x$ lie in $\Omega$.

source.place: Theorem 6.2.1 proof, p.199: explicit rank-one calculation for its Weyl-word induction; enlarged chart from Theorems 4.1.7 and 5.1.13.

proof.text: For a word $n=n_{\alpha_k}\cdots n_{\alpha_1}$ let $p_0=1$, $p_i=n_{\alpha_i}\cdots n_{\alpha_1}$ and $D=\bigcap_{i=0}^k p_i^{-1}\Omega$. On $D$ prove by induction on $i$ that $a(p_i x)=f_N(p_i)a(x)$. For $i=0$ this is the identity. If it holds for $i-1$, both $p_{i-1}x$ and $n_{\alpha_i}p_{i-1}x$ lie in $\Omega$, so step 3 and the homomorphism law of $f_N$ prove the next case. Every geometric fibre of $G$ is irreducible by the identity-component lemma, since it is connected and of finite type. Each translated cell is a nonempty open of that fibre, so $D$ is dense in each fibre of $X=\Omega\cap n^{-1}\Omega$. The latter is smooth over $A$, being open in the smooth group $G$. The fibrewise-density lemma gives $\mathcal O_X\hookrightarrow j_*\mathcal O_D$. Therefore the equality just proved extends to $X$: for each coordinate function of the affine scheme $H$, the two pullbacks agree on $D$, so injectivity makes them equal on $X$, which determines the two morphisms. Torus multiplication preserves $\Omega$ and satisfies $a(tx)=f_T(t)a(x)$ by step 1. Since $n_\alpha^{-1}=\alpha^\vee(-1)^{-1}n_\alpha$ and torus factors move past normalizer factors, the same covariance holds for every finite word in $T(A)$ and $n_\alpha^{\pm1}$, including $n_z^{-1}n_w$.

source.place: Theorem 6.2.1 proof, p.199: explicit prefix induction and extension from a fibrewise dense open; density uses the existing universal-density statement.

proof.text:
On $C_w\cap C_z$ write $x=n_w y$, so $y\in\Omega$ and $(n_z^{-1}n_w)y\in\Omega$. Step 4 gives
$$a_z(x)=f_N(n_z)a((n_z^{-1}n_w)y)=f_N(n_w)a(y)=a_w(x).$$
These are scheme-morphism identities, including on nonreduced intersections. By morphism gluing and step 2 there is a morphism $f:G\to H$ restricting to each $a_w$. In particular $f|_\Omega=a$. We next prove its multiplicativity; it has not been assumed in this gluing.

source.place: Theorem 6.2.1 proof, p.199, open-cell extension; gluing is Stacks Schemes sheaf property as recorded in the cited node.

proof.text:
For a fixed word $n$ as in step 4, the two maps $x\mapsto f(nx)$ and $x\mapsto f_N(n)f(x)$ agree on $\Omega\cap n^{-1}\Omega$. This open is dense in every geometric fibre of $G$, by irreducibility and nonemptiness of translated cells. The fibrewise-density lemma and the affine-coordinate argument of step 4 prove
$$f(nx)=f_N(n)f(x)\quad\text{on }G.$$
Likewise, the two morphisms on $U^-\times_A G$ given by $f(vx)$ and $F_-(v)f(x)$ agree on $U^-\times_A\Omega$ by step 1. Each geometric fibre of the domain is irreducible: $U^-$ is an affine space by root coordinates, and its product with an integral geometric fibre of $G$ is irreducible. This domain is smooth, and that open is fibrewise dense, so the same lemma gives $f(vx)=F_-(v)f(x)$ globally. Applying precisely this argument to $T\times_A G$ and $T\times_A\Omega$ gives $f(tx)=f_T(t)f(x)$. These products are smooth since their first factors are affine space and a split torus, respectively; smoothness and irreducibility can also be checked in their explicit polynomial/Laurent coordinates over $G$.

source.place: Theorem 6.2.1 proof, p.199: extending generator-equivariance from the open cell; universal schematic density replaces any reduced-base argument.

proof.text:
Choose $w_0$ carrying $\Phi^+$ to $-\Phi^+$ from the Bruhat input, and its already chosen word representative $n_0$. For $u\in U^+$ put $v=n_0^{-1}un_0\in U^-$. The ordered root products and normalizer equivariance give
$$F_-(v)=f_N(n_0)^{-1}F_+(u)f_N(n_0).$$
Using step 6 first for $n_0$, then $v$, then $n_0^{-1}$, gives
$$f(ux)=f(n_0 v n_0^{-1}x)=F_+(u)f(x).$$
Consequently, for $q=vtu\in\Omega$, step 6 and this identity give $f(qx)=a(q)f(x)$. For $y=n_w q\in C_w$, apply step 6 once more to obtain
$$f(yx)=f_N(n_w)a(q)f(x)=f(y)f(x).$$
These identities hold as morphisms on $C_w\times_A G$; those opens cover $G\times_A G$. The equality clause of morphism gluing proves multiplicativity everywhere. Restrict it to $(C_w\times_A C_z)\cap\mu^{-1}(C_r)$ to obtain exactly the asserted identity for $a_r,a_w,a_z$. No rank-two homomorphism was used. With empty roots the Bruhat factorization makes $G=T$, the same cover is a singleton and every formula is the given homomorphism $f_N$. All fibrewise-density invocations allow disconnected and nonreduced bases.
